title: Work and kinetic energy
explanation:
Push something along a distance and you do **work** on it: for a constant force along the motion, $W=F\,d$. More generally, work over a small step is the dot product of the force and the displacement [1], so only the part of the force along the motion counts.

The payoff is the work-energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy [2], with $K=\tfrac12 m v^2$. Net work speeds things up; negative net work slows them down, since an object that slows has a negative change in kinetic energy [3].

This lets you skip time entirely. Instead of finding acceleration and duration, add up the work and read off the new speed.
keyIdeas: Kinetic energy $K=\tfrac12mv^2$ grows with the square of speed.

workedExample.problem: A $2$ kg cart starts at rest. A constant net force of $9$ N pushes it $4$ m along a level track. Find the work done and its final speed.
steps: Work-energy theorem: $\Delta K=36$ J, and $K_i=0$, so $K_f=36$ J.
Units check: N·m = J, and J/kg = m²/s².
workedExample.answer: $36$ J of work; final speed $6$ m/s

pitfalls: Forgetting to square the speed in $\tfrac12mv^2$, or dropping the $\tfrac12$.
Counting a force perpendicular to the motion as doing work.
Using one force instead of the net force in the work-energy theorem.
